content:
[Goal]

- Consider making "one of the two cells that share an axis with both placed pieces" clearer by stating:
"On a tic-tac-toe board of size [[n]], two opposing players have each placed a piece at ([[r₁]], [[c₁]]) and ([[r₂]], [[c₂]]) respectively. These two positions are marked with an {{X}} on the board. The best move in this position is to place the next piece at one of ([[r₂]], [[c₁]]) or ([[r₁]], [[c₂]])."

[Constraints]

- Please add that [[r₁]] ≠ [[r₂]] and [[c₁]] ≠ [[c₂]]. You can modify this constraint accordingly however you choose to implement your new test cases according to the suggestions given by @5DN1L.

- Please state that all cell priority values will be distinct.

[Cases]

- Interesting test/validator naming choices... I'm not so sure about the last one. Preferably change it to something less explicit? Perhaps @5DN1L can advise.

Thank you! :)

Goal / Input / Constraints
* Please format "X" as a {{constant}} and remove the quotation marks.

Constraints
* Please change both "{{cell}}" and "cell" to "cell value" (unformatted).

Input
* Please change:

"A list of length n, each list item is a string representing"

to:

"[[n]] space-separated values representing the cells in each row. Each value is either".

Stub generator
* Please change 50 to 2.

Goal
* "Cells that share an axis with both placed pieces" sounds incorrect to me, at least in the case where the pieces are in different rows and columns. In such a case, each candidate cell shares a row with one piece and a column with the other. So, please correct the wording.

* Your comment states "the two points are in the same row or column, in which case, either the highest priority available cell or the highest priority cell between the two pieces is chosen." What if the two pieces are next to each other? There would be no cell between the two pieces.

* Still on the same row/column scenario: there may not be exactly two candidate cells as claimed in the first paragraph of the statement; there may be fewer or more.

Cases
* "The options are (a single digit number n) and (a number < n*10)" is a good idea. Please implement it.

* The current cases appear to be paired based only on grid size (n) only. 

  Assuming
  • The Xs are at (x1, y1) and (x2, y2)
  • y2 > y1
  • Let dx = x2 - x1 and dy = y2 - y1. 
  
  Ignoring same-row and same-column cases, for more systematic and balanced coverage, consider revising the pairing so that each pair shares:

  • the same value of n,

  • the same sign of dx (dx > 0 or dx < 0), and

  • the same relative displacement category:
    - abs(dx) = abs(dy)
    - abs(dx) > abs(dy)
    - abs(dx) < abs(dy)

Thanks.

I am considering including test cases where the two points are in the same row or column, in which case, either the highest priority available cell or the highest priority cell between the two pieces is chosen. 
So long as it doesn't make the puzzle too difficult for a clash, I would like to change the task to: print the board after placing the new piece in the best position.
I am also considering making another version of this for reverse (and maybe shortest mode) where the board is always size 3.
Opinions on any topic would be appreciated.

That was quick.

For the notes on the idea in my comment, I hadn't planned on a test case where they're right next to each other, but that's a good idea. As such, if I were to proceed with that plan, the selection would have to be made from all cells in the grid, which makes sense since you no longer get the benefit of blocking the opponent and extending your line. I could probably take it further and say in that case, find the highest value cell in the row/column that the opponent does not share, so as to extend the line, but I would then have to change the pieces to be player specific, and I also don't want to make it too hard for the average clasher.

For the validator pairing, the first four are basically the test case but rotated, the last four are somewhat random but not entirely. Assuming I understand your suggestion, it would be good to implement. Basically, you're saying the pieces should maintain their relative direction (ie. top piece stays to the left/right of bottom piece in both tests)?

Good point on the naming issue, @User123.

I'm not sure a reference to a gun (9 mm) as a way to convey the grid size is a good idea, or whether everyone would understand that "the sound a German horse makes" refers to 9. I also don't understand why "my daily hotdog intake" means 5; is that meant to be personal or universal?

The contribution guidelines state that the names should "help players quickly understand their purpose". Would the author please rename the cases accordingly?

I'm surprised the gun reference was the problem with that one but fair enough. I wanted to name them just for the sake of it and that's how I usually go about naming things. In all fairness, there is a puzzle on here titled 'Brainfuck'. The hotdog intake is just a reference to a WKUK skit; although, the hotdog intake was higher there, I just couldn't think of something for 5. I guess I'll just go back to the standard names.

@User123 I have already updated the goal statement based on 5DN1L's suggestions. I believe that while your suggestion is an improvement over mine, 5DN1L's is easier to read and understand, but I'm open to changing it again based on other's opinions. I have also changed the constraints to reflect that the rows and columns differ, but I will have to state the priority values constraint as you suggest.

I think I've found a good middle ground with both the case names and the goal statement. All suggestions should be implemented now.
I'm wondering though, is 'Next n Lines: n space-separated values representing the tiles in each row.' accurate? The stub is technically giving each value individually. I had originally hoped for it to be 'for i in range(n): row = input().split()' but I couldn't get it to work. If either of you know how, I'd love to make that change.

The case names look good. I'll review the contribution again a bit later.

The description is correct, because it describes the raw input. Technically the player can parse the raw input however they want.

`loopline` is the only documented keyword for splitting a line and collecting the substrings ( https://www.codingame.com/playgrounds/40701/help-center/stub-generator ). If I remember correctly, someone tried using `array` (undocumented) or a similar keyword, but the stub generator didn't work correctly for every programming language available on CodinGame.

All sections
* "Tile" sounds like a physical object that can be moved around. Consider changing "tile(s)" to "cell(s)" throughout.

Goal
* Totally optional: the word "opposing" could be omitted, as most of us should know that tic-tac-toe isn't a co-operative game 😉

Stub generator
* Please add a write statement, e.g. write answer.

Cases
* The revised cases are better now, though there are still gaps in the coverage:

  ✅ dx > 0, abs(dx) = abs(dy): Pair 1
  ✅ dx > 0, abs(dx) > abs(dy): Pairs 4 & 6
  ❓ dx > 0, abs(dx) < abs(dy): missing
  ❓ dx < 0, abs(dx) = abs(dy): missing
  ✅ dx < 0, abs(dx) > abs(dy): Pairs 3 & 8
  ✅ dx < 0, abs(dx) < abs(dy): Pairs 2, 5 & 7

  Please modify and/or add cases to address the gaps.

  If you're considering modifying cases, please try to keep Pairs 4 and 8 unchanged, as Test 4 and Validator 8 are the only cases where the option with the numerically higher priority is lexicographically smaller (e.g. 13 vs 2).

Thanks.

I've made all the changes. Also, the stub now gives the original line of text instead of splitting. I changed 'it keeps growing' to dx>0, abs(dx)<abs(dy). I replaced 'Hitting the limit' with pair 8 and changed pair 8 to dx<0, abs(dx)=abs(dy).
Both tests of pair 6 should also fail when comparing lexicographically, I haven't changed them, were you managing to pass them without integer conversion?

1. I'd go with the latter wording. I think it's easier to understand, especially for non-native speakers.

2. Having more scenarios (same row / same column / adjacent cells) would add a bit of complexity as you've described. By the way, if you decide *not* to include same-row/column cases, remember to make that explicit in the Constraints section.

3. Yes, that's what I meant for the case pairing: maintain the relative direction of the pieces and their relative displacement (note) in each pair of cases.

Note: It's sufficient that the (in)equality between abs(dx) and abs(dy) to be the same in each pair; the actual values can still differ between the test and the validator. For example, if they're equal, the test could have dx = dy = 3, while the validator has dx = dy = 2.

By the way, please do *not* format "cell" as a {{constant}} in the Constraints section, as it's not a constant.

Too easy, I'll get onto it. Thanks.
Also, if you're wondering what happened to the section about the wording, I realised that I had just copied what you wrote so I figured you'd go with that one and removed it.
